title: Refund idempotency key is built from the RUNNING TOTAL, so a console retry after the 20s timeout refunds the poster twice (and a true double-submit double-debits the earner instead)
summary: The Stripe idempotency key `refund_${pi}_${alreadyRefunded + refundCents}` is derived from `payments.refunded_cents`, which `record_refund` advances. There is therefore NO window in which retrying the same refund is safe: if the first attempt's ledger write landed, the retry builds a DIFFERENT key and issues a second real Stripe refund; if it did not land, the retry builds the SAME key, Stripe dedupes to one refund, and `record_refund` is applied twice. The admin console guarantees this retry happens, because `callPaymentAction` aborts the request at 20s and reports failure while the edge function keeps running to completion.
trigger:
Payment captured at 10000c (earner 9000 / fee 1000). Admin enters 30.00 and clicks Refund.

Branch A (first call slow, completes after the abort): `callPaymentAction` (admin/app/(console)/bookings/actions.ts:76, `AbortSignal.timeout(20_000)`) throws; `run()` catches it, writes an audit row `payment.refund.failed`, and shows the admin an error. The edge function meanwhile completed: Stripe refund R1=3000c, `refunded_cents`=3000. Admin re-enters 30.00 and clicks Refund. Now `alreadyRefunded`=3000, so `remaining`=7000 (passes the guard) and the key is `refund_pi_6000` — a NEW key. Stripe issues R2=3000c with `reverse_transfer:true`. The poster is refunded 6000c for a 3000c decision.

Branch B (double-submit / two operators, both in flight before either `record_refund` commits): both read `alreadyRefunded`=0, both build `refund_pi_3000`, Stripe replays R1 and returns it to both callers, then `record_refund` runs twice under its own row lock: `refunded_cents` 0→3000→6000 and `debit_earnings` fires twice (2×2700c off the earner's `earnings_today/week/total`). Stripe refunded 3000; the ledger says 6000.
money_impact: Branch A: the poster is over-refunded by the full refund amount, and it is taken from the earner (`reverse_transfer:true` pulls 2×2700c out of the earner's connected balance) and from platform fee revenue (2×300c). On a full-amount refund this is a 100% duplicate reversal. Branch B: the earner's in-app earnings are debited twice for one refund, `payments.refunded_cents` overstates by the refund amount, and the poster is then blocked from receiving the rest of a legitimate refund because `remaining = capturedCents - alreadyRefunded` is understated. In both branches the audit log records the refund as FAILED, so the operator's own record contradicts what happened.
evidence:
admin-payment-action/index.ts:190 — `{ idempotencyKey: `refund_${pay.payment_intent_id}_${alreadyRefunded + refundCents}` }` with the comment at :169 claiming "a double-submit cannot refund twice while a genuine second partial refund still goes through".
admin-payment-action/index.ts:154 — `const alreadyRefunded = pay.refunded_cents ?? 0;` (the key input is mutable and advanced by the very call it is meant to make idempotent).
admin-payment-action/index.ts:198 — `await service.rpc('record_refund', { p_payment_id: pay.id, p_cents: refundCents, ... })` runs unconditionally after the (possibly replayed) Stripe call.
supabase/migrations/20260804020000_refund_ledger_fixes.sql:108 — `v_new := v_already + p_cents;` … :123 `perform public.debit_earnings(p_payment_id, v_earner_share);` — additive, with no per-refund idempotency token.
admin/app/(console)/bookings/actions.ts:76 — `signal: AbortSignal.timeout(20_000)` with the comment "the failure is reported as unknown rather than as no" — i.e. the operator is explicitly told to treat an unknown outcome as a failure and retry.
fix_sketch: Key the refund on an operation identity that does not move: mint a refund id (or use the admin_audit_log row id) client-side and pass it as `p_op_id`; use it both as the Stripe idempotency key AND as a UNIQUE column on a new `payment_refunds` row inserted inside `record_refund`, so a replayed Stripe refund cannot produce a second ledger increment and a retried operation cannot produce a second Stripe refund. Also record `refund.id` returned by Stripe in the ledger and reconcile against `charge.refunds` rather than a running total.
verifier_note: Three corrections, all narrowing it. (1) A FULL refund retry is already blocked: after the first attempt `alreadyRefunded == capturedCents`, so `remaining <= 0` and index.ts:156 returns `already_refunded` 409. The exposure exists ONLY on partial refunds and is bounded by the remaining refundable balance — the claim 'on a full-amount refund this is a 100% duplicate reversal' is wrong. (2) The claim 'there is NO window in which retrying the same refund is safe' is false. The explicitly-handled `ledger_desync` path (Stripe refund succeeded, `record_refund` errored, index.ts:219-229) leaves `refunded_cents` unchanged, so a retry rebuilds the SAME key, Stripe replays R1, and the ledger is applied exactly once. That path is safe by construction. (3) Branch B as written is partly wrong: Stripe returns `idempotency_key_in_use` (409) for two genuinely in-flight requests on one key, so the double-ledger variant needs the second invocation to start after the first's `refunds.create` returned but before its `record_refund` COMMITS — a window of tens of milliseconds — and it is then caught by reconcile-stripe's `refund_mismatch` (ours 6000 vs Stripe 3000). The auditor under-sold the one branch that matters: in Branch A, Stripe and the DB both end at 6000, so `reconcile-stripe` (index.ts:161) sees a clean match and NOTHING detects the duplicate. Severity high rather than critical: admin-tier only, needs a >20s stall or a lost response plus an operator retry, and it is capped at the remaining refundable balance. Worth noting separately: the `record_reversal` op (index.ts:120-139) has no idempotency of any kind — a double-click there double-increments `refunded_cents` and double-fires `debit_earnings` with no Stripe call involved at all.

title: `payments.refund_source='admin'` is sticky forever, so every LATER genuine chargeback or Dashboard refund on that payment is silently swallowed by the webhook — disabling the only control that detects unledgered external reversals
summary: `refund_source` is a per-PAYMENT column, written before the Stripe call and never cleared or scoped to the refund that caused it. `recordReversal` in stripe-webhook early-returns for `refund_source === 'admin'` on BOTH `charge.refunded` and `charge.dispute.created`. Once any console refund has touched a payment, that payment can never again produce a `disputes` row from the webhook — and `ctl_external_reversal_not_ledgered` detects unledgered reversals by joining precisely on those `disputes` rows, so the detector goes dark for that payment too.
trigger:
1. Admin partially refunds $10 of a $100 captured charge from the console → `refund_source='admin'` written (index.ts:178) and never reset.
2. Weeks later the poster files a chargeback for the remaining $90 (Stripe allows up to ~120 days). Stripe fires `charge.dispute.created`.
3. `recordReversal` reads `refund_source='admin'` and returns early WITHOUT inserting the `disputes` row (stripe-webhook/index.ts:68-71). The comment justifying the skip only reasons about the console's own `charge.refunded`; it applies the skip to disputes as well.
4. The booking now has no open dispute: it never appears in the console's /disputes queue, and `ctl_external_reversal_not_ledgered` — which starts `from public.disputes dd where dd.reason ilike 'Stripe chargeback%'` — has nothing to join to, so it reports zero violations.
5. reconcile-stripe cannot cover for it: a lost dispute does not increment `charge.amount_refunded`, so its `refund_mismatch` check (ours 1000 vs stripe 1000) passes cleanly, and the payment is in any case outside the 14-day / 200-row scan window by then.
The same sequence with a Stripe-Dashboard refund instead of a chargeback produces the identical blackout.
money_impact: $90 leaves the platform balance and is never written to `payments.refunded_cents`; `debit_earnings` never runs, so the earner's `earnings_total` (and the Tax Center / 1099 basis) still shows money Stripe clawed back. GMV and `admin_dashboard_metrics` permanently overstate revenue by the reversed amount. Nobody is paged: no disputes row, no control finding, no reconciliation hit — the only signal is one best-effort Resend email that a human must notice and act on within Stripe's response deadline, and missing that deadline forfeits the dispute automatically.
evidence:
admin-payment-action/index.ts:178 — `await service.from('payments').update({ refund_source: 'admin' }).eq('id', pay.id);` (no later write ever clears it; `grep -rn refund_source` over the whole repo shows only two writers, both setting a value, never null).
stripe-webhook/index.ts:68 — `if ((payment as { refund_source?: string | null } | null)?.refund_source === 'admin') { ... return bookingId; }` — reached from BOTH the `charge.refunded` and `charge.dispute.created` handlers via `recordReversal`.
supabase/migrations/20260806040000_control_library.sql:332 — `from public.disputes dd where dd.reason ilike 'Stripe refund on charge%' or dd.reason ilike 'Stripe chargeback%'` and :361 `join reversal d on d.booking_id = p.booking_id` — an INNER join, so a payment with no such disputes row is invisible to the control.
supabase/migrations/20260806040000_control_library.sql:649 — the control's own registry text asserts "No false positives from console refunds: … recordReversal early-returns for that source" — i.e. the blackout is load-bearing for the control's design and its permanence was not considered.
fix_sketch: Make the suppression per-EVENT, not per-payment: stamp the specific Stripe refund id (`re_…`) the console created, e.g. `admin_refund_ids text[]`, and have `recordReversal` skip only when the incoming `charge.refunded` refund id is in that list. Never skip on `charge.dispute.created` at all — a chargeback is never operator-initiated. At minimum, clear `refund_source` back to null once the matching `charge.refunded` has been observed.
verifier_note: The mechanism is right; the impact is overstated in two places. (a) 'Nobody is paged' is wrong — `emailAdmin` at stripe-webhook:296-305 fires OUTSIDE `recordReversal` and unconditionally, carrying the dispute id, amount, reason and booking id. The suppressed artifact is the disputes ROW (queue + control), not the alert. (b) The auto-capture-suppression half of the impact is nil here: a console refund requires `pay.status === 'captured'` (admin-payment-action:143), so the money is already settled and `earner-claim-payment`'s `DISPUTE_OPEN` gate (index.ts:167-171) is moot for exactly the payments this bug can touch. (c) The blackout is not strictly 'forever': `record_reversal` overwrites `refund_source` to 'chargeback' (:128), which does not trip the early return, so ledgering one chargeback re-arms the webhook for the next. What genuinely survives is: any external reversal on a payment previously refunded from the console files no `disputes` row, so the /disputes queue and `ctl_external_reversal_not_ledgered` — the designed backstop for a human ignoring the email — are both blind for that payment, and `refunded_cents` / `debit_earnings` are never corrected. That is a fail-open detection guard, not a money-movement defect: medium.

title: `record_reversal` (Record chargeback) writes `refunded_cents` that Stripe can never corroborate, so every correctly-remediated chargeback becomes a permanent, unresolvable CRITICAL reconciliation finding
summary: reconcile-stripe derives "what Stripe says was refunded" solely from `charge.amount_refunded`. A lost chargeback does not create a Refund object and does not increment `amount_refunded` — that is exactly why `record_reversal` exists as a ledger-only path. So the moment an operator uses the console's Record-chargeback button, `ourRefunded > 0` while `realRefundAtStripe == 0`, with `TOLERANCE_CENTS = 0`, and the check fires forever. It cannot be cleared by any action, because both numbers are correct.
trigger: Booking captured at 10000c and later charged back and lost. Operator follows RUNBOOK_MONEY and clicks "Record chargeback" → admin-payment-action op `record_reversal` → `record_refund` sets `payments.refunded_cents = 10000` (index.ts:120-139). Next hourly sweep, reconcile-stripe retrieves the PI: `pi.amount = 10000`, `amount_received = 10000` → `autoReleased = 0`; `charge.amount_refunded = 0` (a dispute is not a refund) → `realRefundAtStripe = 0`; `wasCaptured = true`. `Math.abs(0 - 10000) > 0` → a `refund_mismatch` problem is written via `record_reconciliation_finding` at severity `critical`. The finding is re-asserted on every subsequent run and can never auto-resolve, because the check never stops returning it.
money_impact: No money moves, but this is a detection-integrity defect on the one control that asks the processor instead of the database. Doing the correct thing (ledgering a lost chargeback) manufactures a permanent critical finding on a healthy payment — the exact "permanent-false-positive shape that teaches people to ignore the queue" the file's own comment at :140-152 warns about, and the queue it poisons is the same one that would surface a real `stripe_captured_but_ledger_says_authorized` or `money_captured_on_dead_payment` (an earner unpaid on captured money). It also creates a standing incentive for operators to skip the Record-chargeback button, which reintroduces the exact GMV overstatement `ctl_external_reversal_not_ledgered` was built to catch.
evidence:
supabase/functions/reconcile-stripe/index.ts:158-169 — `const realRefundAtStripe = Math.max(0, refundedAtStripe - autoReleased);` … `if (wasCaptured && Math.abs(realRefundAtStripe - ourRefunded) > TOLERANCE_CENTS)` with `const TOLERANCE_CENTS = 0` (:33).
supabase/functions/reconcile-stripe/index.ts:72 — the select list is `"id, booking_id, payment_intent_id, amount_cents, fee_cents, earner_amount_cents, refunded_cents, status, captured_at, created_at"` — `refund_source` is NOT read, so the function has no way to tell a ledgered chargeback from a real desync.
supabase/functions/admin-payment-action/index.ts:114-139 — `record_reversal` … "This is the ledger-only path: no Stripe call, same accounting, distinctly labelled." — the distinct label (`refund_source='chargeback'`, :128) exists but reconcile-stripe never consults it.
supabase/migrations/20260806040000_control_library.sql:649 — "a lost chargeback, which Stripe will not even let refunds.create touch" — confirms no Refund object is created, hence `amount_refunded` stays 0.
fix_sketch: Select `refund_source` in reconcile-stripe and add Stripe's own dispute total to the expected side: `expectedAtStripe = realRefundAtStripe + sum(charge.disputes/balance-transaction withdrawals)`, or exclude `refund_source='chargeback'` rows from the `refund_mismatch` check and cover them with a dedicated chargeback-reconciliation check driven by `stripe.disputes.list`. Same subtraction discipline the function already applies for `autoReleased`.
verifier_note: 'Permanent' and 'unresolvable' are both wrong, and the trigger is much narrower than stated. (a) reconcile-stripe scans only `created_at >= now() - 14 days`, newest 200 (:65-74). Card chargebacks typically arrive 30-90 days after the charge, by which time the payment row is outside the window and NO finding is ever produced. The defect only manifests when the operator records the reversal while the payment is still inside the 14-day/200-row window. (b) Once it does fire, it stops being re-asserted the moment the payment ages out — and because `resolve_reconciliation_findings` was scoped to `p_examined` by `20260806270000_resolve_only_examined.sql`, it is not auto-closed either, so it sits open until an operator clicks it away. `resolveFinding` (`admin/app/(console)/controls/actions.ts:20-41`) closes it permanently at that point; a manual resolve *inside* the window does get re-opened hourly, because `record_reconciliation_finding`'s ON CONFLICT is partial on `resolved_at is null` (`20260806130000:70-84`) and therefore inserts a fresh row. Net effect: a bounded, at-most-14-day noisy critical finding on a subset of chargebacks, clearable by hand afterwards — a queue-hygiene defect, not a standing detection blackout. Low.

title: CANCELLABLE_STATUSES does not close the accept-then-void hole: `pending` is not a hold-free state, and accept-booking's unconditional `payments.status='authorized'` write can resurrect a row the poster just cancelled
summary: `stripe-create-payment-intent` writes `payments.status='authorized'` with a live `requires_capture` PaymentIntent while the booking is STILL `pending` — the hold is placed before accept, not by it. `stripe-cancel-payment` permits `pending`, so both parties can void a real, funded authorization in that window with a plain user token. `accept-booking` then writes `payments.status='authorized'` with no status predicate and never re-reads the PaymentIntent after the write, so a cancel that lands between its `paymentIntents.retrieve` and that update leaves a CONFIRMED booking whose payments row reads `authorized` against a canceled PaymentIntent — the precise 'looks funded, isn't' state the CANCELLABLE_STATUSES guard was added to prevent.
trigger: Poster wants free work. (1) Poster's client calls stripe-create-payment-intent and confirms the card → PI is `requires_capture`, `payments.status='authorized'` (create-payment-intent:405), booking still `pending`. (2) Poster calls accept-booking. It reads the booking (`pending`, ok), reads the payment, and retrieves the PI → `requires_capture` ✓ (accept-booking:66). (3) In that gap the poster fires stripe-cancel-payment with their own token: booking status is `pending`, which IS in CANCELLABLE_STATUSES (:67); `started_at` is null (:77); payment status is `authorized`, so neither the `cancelled` (:90) nor `captured` (:95) early-return fires → `stripe.paymentIntents.cancel()` runs (:99) and the row is stamped `cancelled` (:101). (4) accept-booking resumes and executes `update({ status: 'authorized' }).eq('id', payment.id)` (accept-booking:75) — no `.eq('status', …)` predicate — overwriting `cancelled`, then flips the booking to `confirmed`. Final state: booking `confirmed`, `payments.status='authorized'`, PaymentIntent CANCELED at Stripe. If the race is lost, accept-booking returns HOLD_NOT_AUTHORIZED, the poster re-places the hold and retries — unlimited attempts, no rate limit on either endpoint.
money_impact: The earner sees an accepted, funded gig (neither client reads the `payments` table; both infer escrow from `bookings.status`), does the work, and there is nothing to capture: stripe-capture-payment returns HOLD_EXPIRED and earner-claim-payment returns HOLD_EXPIRED. The worker performs the full gig for $0 and the poster pays nothing. Detection exists but is after the fact and out of band — reconcile-stripe's `hold_dead_at_stripe` check (index.ts:172) fires on the next hourly sweep — so the loss is prevented only if a human intervenes before the work is done.
evidence:
supabase/functions/stripe-cancel-payment/index.ts:67 — `const CANCELLABLE_STATUSES = ['pending', 'declined', 'cancelled'];` with the comment at :64 claiming it mirrors admin/lib/deleteUser.ts's contract "Only holds on un-started bookings may be voided".
supabase/functions/stripe-create-payment-intent/index.ts:397-406 — `await supabase.from('payments').upsert({ booking_id, payment_intent_id: pi.id, … status: 'authorized', … })` — written at PI creation, i.e. while `canHold` accepted `booking.status` of `'pending'` (:99).
supabase/functions/accept-booking/index.ts:4 — "The poster calls this after authorizing the card client-side" — confirms the hold precedes the accept.
supabase/functions/accept-booking/index.ts:75 — `await supabase.from('payments').update({ status: 'authorized' }).eq('id', payment.id);` — no status precondition, in contrast to the very next statement (:81-82) which DOES guard the bookings write with `.eq('status', 'pending')` for exactly this class of interleaving.
supabase/functions/stripe-cancel-payment/index.ts:38 — `if (booking.job?.poster_id !== user.id && booking.earner_id !== user.id) return 403;` — the poster is an authorized caller.
fix_sketch: Two changes, either of which breaks the race, both worth making. (a) In accept-booking, make the payments write conditional and verify after: `.update({status:'authorized'}).eq('id', payment.id).in('status', ['pending','authorized']).select()`, then re-retrieve the PaymentIntent AFTER the bookings flip and roll the booking back to `pending` if it is no longer `requires_capture`. (b) In stripe-cancel-payment, stop treating `pending` as hold-free: reject when the PaymentIntent is `requires_capture` and the caller is the poster, or require the booking row to be moved to `cancelled`/`declined` first (the same ordering cancelBooking already uses) so `pending` never appears in CANCELLABLE_STATUSES.
verifier_note: The auditor missed a self-healing layer that materially changes the exploit. Cancelling the PI fires `payment_intent.canceled`, a REQUIRED webhook event (stripe-webhook:5), and that handler (:192-226) both stamps `payments` 'cancelled' where `status='authorized'` AND demotes a `confirmed` booking with `earner_done = false` back to `pending`. It lands seconds after the cancel and undoes precisely the end-state in the trigger. So the attacker must win a SECOND, much narrower race — the webhook's bookings read must land before accept-booking's confirm write — and every lost attempt heals itself (booking back to pending, poster must re-authorize). Two further corrections: (1) the truly undetected residual is booking='confirmed' + payments='cancelled' + PI canceled, which no SQL control covers (`ctl_money_exposed_on_dead_booking` needs the booking declined/cancelled; `ctl_escrow_hold_lapsed_uncancelled`, redefined last in `20260806150000_authorized_at.sql:40`, needs `p.status='authorized'`) and which reconcile-stripe also misses, since check 4b only fires on a cancelled payment with `receivedCents > 0`. The variant the auditor describes (payments left 'authorized') is the DETECTED one — reconcile-stripe's `hold_dead_at_stripe` (:182) catches it on the next hourly sweep. (2) Fix sketch (b) is not viable as written: `__tests__/cancelPaymentContract.test.js:43-49` explicitly asserts `pending` IS in CANCELLABLE_STATUSES because `declineBooking` calls this function while the booking is still pending. Only fix (a) — a status-predicated payments write in accept-booking plus a post-confirm PI re-read — is compatible with the pinned contract. Medium: reachable and unpinned, but gated behind two sub-second races with an automatic heal on failure.

title: Settlement is gated on a cached `onboarded` flag that any earner app-open can flip to false, and neither settle path re-verifies live — the hold then lapses and the worker is unpaid
summary: stripe-capture-payment and earner-claim-payment refuse to move money when `stripe_accounts.onboarded` is false, but they read only the cached column. The only thing that can flip it back to true is the earner manually opening EarnScreen/ProfileScreen/PayoutSetup (which calls stripe-connect-status). The identical live-Stripe re-verification already exists in stripe-create-payment-intent but was not carried to the two paths that actually have a deadline.
trigger: Earner finishes a gig; a real escrow hold is live. Stripe re-verifies the Express account (routine in live mode — a new `currently_due`, a `pending_verification`, or a bank-account rejection flips `payouts_enabled` to false for hours or days). The earner opens the app: EarnScreen.js:88 calls getPayoutStatus() -> stripe-connect-status, which at index.ts:55-60 writes `onboarded = false` to the row as a side effect of a READ. From that moment: poster taps Verify & Rate -> stripe-capture-payment returns 409 EARNER_PAYOUTS_DISABLED; earner taps claim -> earner-claim-payment returns the same 409 (index.ts:207). Neither party can do anything. Stripe auto-cancels the uncaptured authorization at ~7 days; the webhook marks the payments row 'cancelled' and every subsequent attempt returns HOLD_EXPIRED (stripe-capture-payment/index.ts:98-103, earner-claim-payment/index.ts:190-192).
money_impact: The earner performed the work and receives nothing; the poster's card hold is released, so the money is never collected either. Recovery requires the poster to voluntarily re-run the recovery re-hold (stripe-create-payment-intent/index.ts:98-100) AND still have a card on file — in the ghosting scenario earner-claim-payment exists for, the poster is by definition gone. Confirmed by exhaustive grep: no cron job, no control, and reconcile-stripe (which only reads `payments`) ever refreshes this flag server-side.
evidence: stripe-capture-payment/index.ts:116-125 — `if (payment.status !== 'captured') { const { data: earnerAcct } = await supabase.from('stripe_accounts').select('onboarded').eq('user_id', booking.earner_id).single(); if (!earnerAcct?.onboarded) { return json({ error: 'EARNER_PAYOUTS_DISABLED', ... }, 409); } }` — cached column only, no `stripe.accounts.retrieve`. Same at earner-claim-payment/index.ts:205-209. Contrast stripe-create-payment-intent/index.ts:117-125 which DOES retrieve live: `if (!earnerOnboarded && earnerAcct?.account_id) { const acc = await stripe.accounts.retrieve(earnerAcct.account_id); earnerOnboarded = !!(acc.details_submitted && acc.charges_enabled && acc.payouts_enabled); ... }`. The demoting writer is stripe-connect-status/index.ts:55-60: `if (status.onboarded !== acct.onboarded) { await supabase.from('stripe_accounts').update({ onboarded: status.onboarded }).eq('account_id', acct.account_id); }`, reached from src/screens/EarnScreen.js:88 `getPayoutStatus().then(setPayoutStatus)`.
fix_sketch: Lift the live re-check out of stripe-create-payment-intent into _shared (e.g. `assertPayoutCapable(stripe, supabase, userId)`) and call it from stripe-capture-payment and earner-claim-payment before returning EARNER_PAYOUTS_DISABLED — retrieve the account, sync the flag both ways, and only refuse if Stripe itself still says no. Separately, do not let a settle-path refusal be silent: when a hold is blocked by EARNER_PAYOUTS_DISABLED, file a control finding so the ~7-day expiry is visible before it fires.
verifier_note: Two corrections to the mechanism and one to the impact. (1) The demotion is not spurious. stripe-connect-status writes false ONLY when a live `stripe.accounts.retrieve` says the account is not payout-capable, so at the moment of the write the 409 is the intended fail-closed behaviour, not a bug. The actual failing state is a stale-FALSE: Stripe re-enables the account and nothing refreshes the cache. That is a narrower window than 'any app-open flips it to false'. (2) The earner-claim leg is largely self-healed by the screen that hosts the button. src/screens/EarnScreen.js:87-89 runs `getPayoutStatus().then(setPayoutStatus)` on mount — that is stripe-connect-status, i.e. a live retrieve that syncs the flag both ways — and the 'Claim payment' action is at EarnScreen.js:423 on that same screen. An earner cannot reach the claim button without having mounted the screen that just re-synced the flag live (residual: a tab screen that stays mounted for days, since the effect deps are `[]`). The surviving leg is the poster-initiated capture, where the poster's app has no reason to refresh the earner's flag. (3) The failure is NOT invisible, so the second half of the fix_sketch already exists: ctl_escrow_hold_expiring_work_done (final definition supabase/migrations/20260806150000_authorized_at.sql:66-87) selects exactly `p.status='authorized' and b.status in ('completed','verified')` between 5 and 8 days of `authorized_at` — precisely the blocked-capture state — and controls_sweep_and_page runs hourly and pages on findings newly opened in the last 90 minutes. A human is paged roughly two days before Stripe cancels the authorization.

title: stripe-connect-onboard creates the Stripe account with no idempotency key and discards the insert error — two concurrent calls orphan a fully-KYC'd Connect account the platform can never reach
summary: The get-or-create is a non-atomic read-then-write. `stripe.accounts.create` carries no idempotency key (every PaymentIntent create in this codebase does), and the result of the follow-up `insert` is never checked, so a primary-key collision on `user_id` is silent and the function still returns an onboarding link for the account that lost the race.
trigger: Two overlapping POSTs from one user — a double-tap on PayoutSetupScreen's "Set up payouts", or a client retry on a slow response. Both requests read no row at index.ts:99-104 (`.single()` returns data:null on zero rows), both call `stripe.accounts.create` at index.ts:167 producing acct_A and acct_B, both call `insert` at index.ts:201. One succeeds; the other violates the `user_id` primary key (migration_stripe.sql:15) and returns an error that is discarded. That request still returns `{ url, accountId: acct_B }` at index.ts:216. The earner opens that link and completes full KYC — SSN, DOB, photo ID, bank account — on acct_B. The DB holds acct_A, which was never onboarded.
money_impact: Every money path resolves the earner by `stripe_accounts.user_id` (stripe-create-payment-intent/index.ts:106-110, stripe-tip/index.ts:56, stripe-capture-payment/index.ts:118), so all of them see acct_A and return EARNER_NO_PAYOUT. The poster cannot accept the booking and the earner cannot be paid, while the earner's Stripe return page told them setup was complete. acct_B is an orphan connected account holding the earner's government ID and bank details that no code path can ever reach, delete, or reconcile. Recovery requires the earner to re-submit full KYC a second time on acct_A.

title: ctl_stripe_id_mode_mismatch's length predicates match every real Stripe account and customer id, so the control designated "the single most likely way the live cutover breaks" will fire on 100% of rows and detect nothing
summary: The control tries to spot test-mode ids left behind after the live-key cutover using `length(account_id) < 22` and `length(customer_id) < 19`. Stripe account ids are 21 characters and customer ids are 18 characters in BOTH modes, so both predicates are always true. Once app_flags.stripe_mode flips to 'live', the control emits a critical finding for every connected account and every customer, including correctly-created live ones.
trigger: Operator follows PRE_LAUNCH_DATA_RESET.md §5, deletes the stale rows, flips STRIPE_SECRET_KEY to sk_live_ and sets app_flags.stripe_mode='live'. The first earner completes live payout onboarding, producing a legitimate live id of the shape `acct_1ThvnME0UZFlVCOp` (21 chars). The next hourly `controls_sweep_and_page` run evaluates `a.account_id like 'acct_1%' and length(a.account_id) < 22` -> true -> a new open finding in control_findings, severity 'critical', domain 'money'. Because findings are unique on (control_key, entity_id) and the sweep pages only when something NEWLY needs a human, every new earner and every new poster who saves a card generates a fresh critical page, permanently.
money_impact: No money moves wrongly by itself, but the detection layer for the failure the codebase itself calls "the single most likely way the live cutover breaks" is destroyed: a genuinely stale test-mode id is indistinguishable from the hundreds of correct live ids in the same finding set. The predictable operator response is to disable or ignore the control, at which point a real stale acct_/cus_ id survives to fail silently at the moment a poster tries to pay. This violates the codebase's own stated doctrine that a control which stops telling the truth is as serious as a violation.
evidence: supabase/migrations/20260806350000_controls_always_on.sql:192 — `where mode.m = 'live' and a.account_id like 'acct_1%' and length(a.account_id) < 22` and :199 — `where mode.m = 'live' and c.customer_id like 'cus_%' and length(c.customer_id) < 19`. The repo's own sample id, RUNBOOK_MONEY.md:188, is `acct_1ThvnME0UZFlVCOp` = 21 characters, which satisfies `< 22`; live-mode account ids share that format and length. The registry entry at :240-247 rates it `'critical', 'money'` with the rationale `'There are connected accounts and customers holding test ids today, which makes this the most likely way the live cutover breaks.'`
fix_sketch: Length is not a mode signal for acct_/cus_ ids — the two modes are format-identical. Detect mode by asking Stripe: have reconcile-stripe (which already holds STRIPE_SECRET_KEY and already writes control_findings) attempt `accounts.retrieve` / `customers.retrieve` on each stored id and file a finding on a `resource_missing` error. That is the only test that actually distinguishes the two universes. Failing that, stamp the mode on the row at insert time (`stripe_accounts.stripe_mode`) from the key in use and compare against app_flags.
verifier_note: The predicted symptom is the less likely of the two, and the real one is worse. `app_flags.stripe_mode` is never seeded: grep across supabase/, admin/ and every .md returns only the two lines inside the control itself, and PRE_LAUNCH_DATA_RESET.md §5 (lines 169-182) tells the operator to `delete from stripe_accounts; delete from stripe_customers;` and flip the keys without ever mentioning the flag. With `coalesce(..., 'test')` as the default, both arms of the union are gated on `mode.m = 'live'` and return zero rows FOREVER unless someone sets an undocumented flag by hand. So the likely outcome is not a permanent critical page — it is a control that silently reports 'all clear' at exactly the cutover it was written to guard, which is the failure mode the codebase's own doctrine calls out (trg_notify_safety_report dead for a month on unassertable config). Either way the control detects nothing: dormant if the flag is never set, tautological if it is. Held at medium rather than dropped: no money moves wrongly, but this is a money-domain guard that fails open, and the missing runbook step should be part of any fix.

title: The payout-readiness gate requires `charges_enabled`, which a destination charge does not need, and onboarding requests the `card_payments` capability that produces it — an earner who can be paid is told they cannot be
summary: `onboarded = details_submitted && charges_enabled && payouts_enabled`. In the destination-charge model the platform is the merchant of record; the connected account only needs the `transfers` capability to receive funds. `charges_enabled` reflects the `card_payments` capability, which this platform never uses — but stripe-connect-onboard requests it anyway, importing card_payments' entire requirement set into every earner's account and into the settlement gate.
trigger: An earner's `card_payments` capability goes inactive or back to pending — Stripe re-reviews it independently of transfers, and it is the capability that carries the mcc / url / product_description / statement-descriptor requirements this very file works around at index.ts:39-44 and 129-142. `transfers` stays active and `payouts_enabled` stays true, so the account can receive a destination charge and pay it out to the bank. But `account.charges_enabled` is false, so deriveConnectStatus returns `onboarded: false`, stripe-connect-status writes false to the row, and stripe-capture-payment/index.ts:119 and earner-claim-payment/index.ts:207 both return 409 EARNER_PAYOUTS_DISABLED on a live hold.
money_impact: The earner has done the work, Stripe would accept the transfer, and the platform refuses to release it. The hold ages out at ~7 days and the earner is unpaid. The same over-strict gate also blocks the earner from ever opening their Express dashboard to fix anything: stripe-payout-login-link/index.ts:35 returns NOT_ONBOARDED on the same flag. The requested-but-unused card_payments capability is also what forces the BUSINESS_PROFILE prefill hack in stripe-connect-onboard — the code is working around a requirement it opted into.
evidence: supabase/functions/_shared/connectStatus.ts:127-129 — `// Keep IDENTICAL to the gate in stripe-create-payment-intent ... const onboarded = detailsSubmitted && chargesEnabled && payoutsEnabled;`. stripe-connect-onboard/index.ts:171-174 — `capabilities: { card_payments: { requested: true }, transfers: { requested: true } }`. The only place a connected account is used is `transfer_data: { destination: earnerAcct.account_id }` (stripe-create-payment-intent/index.ts:377, stripe-tip/index.ts:122) — a destination charge, never a direct charge and never `on_behalf_of`, so `card_payments` on the connected account is never exercised. stripe-payout-login-link/index.ts:35 — `if (!acct.onboarded) return json({ error: 'NOT_ONBOARDED', ... }, 400);`
fix_sketch: Stop requesting `card_payments` in stripe-connect-onboard — request `transfers` only. Redefine the settlement gate as `details_submitted && payouts_enabled && account.capabilities.transfers === 'active'`, keeping charges_enabled out of it entirely (it can still feed the UI's `state` for messaging). Drop the `onboarded` precondition on stripe-payout-login-link: an earner whose account has a problem is exactly the person who needs the Express dashboard.
verifier_note: Downgraded from medium to low, and one part of the money_impact is stronger than stated while the trigger is weaker. Weaker trigger: the failing path needs Stripe to hold `card_payments` inactive while `transfers` stays active AND `payouts_enabled` stays true. Capabilities do have independent requirement sets, so this is possible, but for a US individual Express account requesting both, the requirement sets largely overlap and Stripe usually disables payouts alongside — how often the divergence actually occurs is a Stripe-runtime question I cannot settle from the repo, and it is the only thing separating this from a purely theoretical over-strictness. It is also not a silent loss: the resulting stuck hold lands squarely in ctl_escrow_hold_expiring_work_done (20260806150000_authorized_at.sql:66-87, booking 'completed' + payment 'authorized', 5-8 days) and pages hourly. Stronger than stated: the dead-end is worse than the finding says. stripe-connect-onboard:123-126 early-returns `{ alreadyOnboarded, status }` with NO account link when the state is 'restricted' or 'pending', and stripe-payout-login-link:35 returns NOT_ONBOARDED on the same flag — so a restricted earner has no path to Stripe at all, neither onboarding nor the Express dashboard. The fix (request `transfers` only, gate on `details_submitted && payouts_enabled && capabilities.transfers === 'active'`, drop the `onboarded` precondition on the login link) is correct on all three counts.

title: settle_booking_benefits refunds a poster-discount campaign's entire reserve at capture, so budget_cents never binds and burn-down reads $0
summary: settle_booking_benefits() measures the true cost of EVERY promo_redemptions row with promo_benefit_cents(), which is a fee-override counterfactual: fee(amount, standing_rate) - fee(amount, r.fee_bps). For a poster_discount redemption r.fee_bps IS the booking's own pinned rate, so the difference is 0. `actual` therefore comes out 0, `delta = 0 - reserved_cents` is the full negative reserve, and promotions.spent_cents is decremented back to where it started on every captured booking — while the poster really was charged less and the platform really did absorb the discount. The one ceiling the design calls structural (budget_cents) is un-spent on every successful redemption.
trigger:
Create a poster_discount campaign (kind='poster_discount', poster_discount_cents=500, budget_cents=25000, max_redemptions=100, max_benefit_cents=15000 — the table defaults). Poster holds a grant; earner books a $100 gig at the standing 1000 bps with no tier, no fee_override, no fee credit.

1. pin_booking_amount -> consume_poster_discount: poster_discount_headroom(10000,1000) = platform_fee_cents(10000,1000)=1000 minus floor (ceil(290)+30+25=345) = 655. hit = least(500, 655, 15000) = 500. promo_redemptions row written with reserved_cents=500, fee_bps=1000. promotions.spent_cents 0 -> 500, redemptions_used 0 -> 1. bookings.poster_discount_cents = 500.
2. Poster accepts: authorizedCents = 10000-500 = 9500, application_fee = 1000-500 = 500. The poster is really charged $95 instead of $100; the platform's margin on the booking drops by 500c.
3. Poster verifies -> stripe-capture-payment/index.ts:241 calls settle_booking_benefits(booking, capturedGigCents=10000).
4. promo_benefit_cents(10000, r.fee_bps=1000) = platform_fee_cents(10000, fee_bps_at(now())=1000) - platform_fee_cents(10000, 1000) = 1000 - 1000 = 0. actual = least(15000, 0) = 0. delta = -500. promotions.spent_cents = greatest(0, 500-500) = 0. promo_redemptions.benefit_cents = 0, settled_at = now().

Repeat: spent_cents returns to 0 after every capture, so `spent_cents + hit <= budget_cents` in consume_poster_discount can never fail. Only max_redemptions still bounds the campaign.
money_impact: The platform pays every poster discount out of its own margin while the campaign's budget records zero spend. Real exposure becomes max_redemptions x per-use discount instead of budget_cents. With the table defaults that is 100 x $5 = $500 against a $250 budget (2x). An operator who bounds a campaign the documented way — a small budget with a generous max_redemptions, e.g. budget $250 / max_redemptions 5000 / $5 discount — is exposed to $25,000 against a $250 cap (100x). It is also silent: /promotions (admin/app/(console)/promotions/page.tsx:95,113) and the dashboard tile (admin/app/(console)/page.tsx:92) both render spent_cents, so the burn-down bar sits at $0.00 forever. No control fires: ctl_redemption_double_charge only compares redemptions_used (1) to row count (1); ctl_discount_charged_not_delivered needs reserved_cents (500, untouched by settle) > delivered (500); ctl_benefit_never_settled needs settled_at null, which settle just stamped; ctl_poster_discount_underwater needs discount+credit > headroom (500 <= 655).
evidence:
supabase/migrations/20260806220000_benefit_lifecycle.sql:72-83 (the counterfactual is fee-override-only, with no notion of a discount):
  create or replace function public.promo_benefit_cents(p_amount_cents integer, p_fee_bps integer)
  ... select greatest(0,
      public.platform_fee_cents(p_amount_cents, public.fee_bps_at(now()))
    - public.platform_fee_cents(p_amount_cents, p_fee_bps))

supabase/migrations/20260806220000_benefit_lifecycle.sql:163-192 (settle applies it to EVERY redemption row, with no `kind` branch):
  for r in select * from public.promo_redemptions
     where booking_id = p_booking and released_at is null and settled_at is null for update
  loop
    actual := least(
      coalesce((select max_benefit_cents from public.promotions where id = r.promotion_id), r.reserved_cents),
      public.promo_benefit_cents(p_amount_cents, r.fee_bps));
    delta := actual - r.reserved_cents;
    update public.promotions set spent_cents = greatest(0, spent_cents + delta) where id = r.promotion_id;
    update public.promo_redemptions set benefit_cents = actual, settled = true, settled_at = now() where id = r.id;

supabase/migrations/20260806340000_discount_kind_confusion.sql:151-155 (the redemption's fee_bps for a poster discount is the booking's own rate, which is exactly what makes the difference zero):
  insert into public.promo_redemptions
    (grant_id, promotion_id, user_id, booking_id, fee_bps, reserved_cents)
  values (g.id, p.id, p_user, p_booking, coalesce(p_fee_bps, 1000), hit)

supabase/migrations/20260806320000_discount_headroom_after_credit.sql:196-200 (p_fee_bps passed in is new.fee_bps_quoted, the booking's pinned rate)

supabase/migrations/20260806070000_promotions.sql:65-72 (the ceilings this defeats: max_redemptions default 100, budget_cents default 25000, max_benefit_cents default 15000)

Final-definition check: `grep -rln "function public.settle_booking_benefits" supabase/migrations/` returns only 20260806220000_benefit_lifecycle.sql; same for promo_benefit_cents. consume_poster_discount's final definition is 20260806340000.
fix_sketch: Branch on the promotion kind inside settle_booking_benefits. For kind='poster_discount' the true cost is not a rate counterfactual at all — it is the discount actually delivered, scaled to what was captured: actual := least(max_benefit_cents, round(r.reserved_cents::numeric * p_amount_cents / nullif(b.amount_cents_quoted,0))), or simply r.reserved_cents on a full capture. Only kind='fee_override' should route through promo_benefit_cents. Add a control that asserts promotions.spent_cents >= sum(reserved_cents) for settled, unreleased poster_discount redemptions — ctl_redemption_double_charge deliberately compares counts only and cannot see a spend that was handed back.
verifier_note:
Mechanism is right; two refinements and one severity correction.

(1) The refund is exactly -reserved_cents only when fee_bps_quoted equals the standing rate at capture — the common case. If a loyalty rung is ever enabled, r.fee_bps < fee_bps_at(now()) and `actual` becomes fee(standing) - fee(tier), a number with no relationship to the discount that can land either side of reserved_cents. So the defect is 'the campaign's spend is set to an unrelated figure', of which 'zeroed' is the default-configuration instance, not merely 'always refunded'.

(2) Scope is narrower than 'EVERY promo_redemptions row'. fee_override redemptions route through promo_benefit_cents correctly — on a full capture actual == reserved and the settle is a correct no-op. Referral bonuses never write promo_redemptions at all (they use bonus_ledger, 20260806250000:70-76). The defect is specific to kind='poster_discount'.

(3) Severity high, not critical. No money is created, destroyed, double-paid or stolen, and no party is charged or paid an amount they did not agree to: each per-booking discount is still clamped by poster_discount_headroom minus the fee credit, so the platform can never be pushed below Stripe cost. What is lost is one of the two ceilings the design calls structural — lifetime exposure becomes max_redemptions x per-use discount instead of budget_cents — spent silently, with the console burn-down (admin/app/(console)/promotions/page.tsx) reading $0.

Note for the fix: earner-claim-payment does NOT call settle, so poster-discount bookings settled through the ghost path currently keep the CORRECT spend. Adding the settle call there (finding 2's fix sketch) without the kind branch would extend this bug to that path.

title: earner-claim-payment captures money but never settles the promo redemption, leaving a campaign permanently charged the worst-case reserve
summary: The reserve-at-booking / settle-at-capture contract that 20260806220000 introduced is only honoured by stripe-capture-payment (index.ts:241). earner-claim-payment — the earner's self-service settlement when the poster ghosts — captures the hold, writes the split, credits earnings and advances the booking to 'verified', but never calls settle_booking_benefits. The redemption stays at reserved_cents forever with settled_at NULL, so the campaign's budget keeps holding the worst-case figure against work that finished at a known, usually lower, price.
trigger: Earner holds a fee_override grant and books a gig; consume_promo_grant charges the campaign hit = least(max_benefit_cents, promo_benefit_cents(amount_quoted, grant_bps)) and writes a promo_redemptions row. The poster accepts, the earner does the work, the poster never verifies. After the grace window the earner calls earner-claim-payment, which captures at Stripe, writes status='captured' + earner_amount_cents + fee_cents (index.ts:285-290), calls credit_earnings (:293) and sets bookings.status='verified' (:302-304). No settle_booking_benefits call exists anywhere in the file. promotions.spent_cents keeps the reserve; promo_redemptions.benefit_cents stays 0 and settled_at stays NULL.
money_impact: The campaign's budget is over-consumed by (reserved_cents - actual_benefit) for every booking settled through the ghost path, so a campaign exhausts before its budget is really spent and later users are silently refused the benefit they were promised (consume_promo_grant returns null when `spent_cents + hit <= budget_cents` fails, and the booking then prices at the standing rate). It is at least visible: ctl_benefit_never_settled fires on any redemption with released_at/settled_at NULL on a booking in ('verified','declined','cancelled') older than 2h — which is precisely this shape — so the cost is an operator ticket per ghosted promoted booking rather than a silent leak.
fix_sketch: After the credit_earnings call, mirror stripe-capture-payment: `await supabase.rpc('settle_booking_benefits', { p_booking: bookingId, p_amount_cents: capturedCents + poster_discount_cents })`, non-fatal and logged, so the same immutable-input derivation is used and a retry is a no-op (settled_at already set filters the row out of the loop).
verifier_note:
The missing call is real; the consequence is operational, not monetary. Correct impact: (a) every promoted booking settled through the ghost path leaves a permanent OPEN ctl_benefit_never_settled finding — a high-severity money control that pages hourly via controls_sweep_and_page — so the cost is a recurring false page that trains operators to ignore a money control, not budget over-consumption; (b) promo_redemptions.benefit_cents stays 0 and settled=false forever on those rows, so any reporting built on benefit_cents understates real benefit cost. Budget over-consumption requires a partial capture (handled by the other path) or a standing-rate change in the accept-to-claim window. Severity low.

The proposed fix is actively dangerous as written: given finding 1, adding an unconditional settle_booking_benefits call here would import the poster-discount reserve-refund into the ghost path, which is currently the only capture path that accounts poster discounts correctly. Fix finding 1's kind branch first, then add the call.

title: The assistant's take-home mirror maps a legitimately pinned 0 bps to 10%, understating earnings on every promoted or 0%-tier booking
summary: assistant/index.ts reimplements platform_fee_cents inline as `netOf()` and coerces the rate with `Number.isFinite(Number(feeBps)) && Number(feeBps) > 0 ? trunc : DEFAULT_FEE_BPS`. A pinned fee_bps_quoted of 0 — exactly what a "first 2 gigs free" promotion (promotions.fee_bps check allows 0) and a 0% loyalty rung (fee_tiers.fee_bps check allows 0) store — is not > 0, so it falls back to 1000 bps. This is the identical `> 0` vs `>= 0` defect that safeBps() in the three money edge functions was explicitly rewritten to fix; the assistant copy was left behind.
trigger: An earner completes a $100 gig on a booking whose pin is fee_bps_quoted = 0 (0% promo grant or a 0-bps fee tier). Ask the assistant about earnings/goal progress. netOf(100, 0): the `> 0` test fails, bps becomes 1000, pct = trunc((10000*1000+5000)/10000) = 1000, floor = ceil(290)+30+25 = 345, fee = max(1000, 345) = 1000, reported net = $90.00. What the earner was actually charged is platform_fee_after_credit(10000, 0, 0) = max(345, platform_fee_cents(10000,0)=345) = 345, so real net = $96.55. The assistant reports $6.55 less on that booking, and the same understated figure feeds `earned`, `avg` and the monthly-goal advice.
money_impact: No money moves wrongly, but the number the product tells the earner they took home differs from what they were actually paid, in the direction that makes the platform's flagship 0% incentive look like it was never applied. Same disclosure class as the pinned-vs-current-rate rule: shared/pricing.js coerceBps() gets this right (`Number.isFinite(n) ? Math.trunc(n) : DEFAULT`, so 0 stays 0) and all three money edge functions get it right, so the app and the assistant quote different take-home for the same booking — which is the exact divergence the comment block above netOf says it exists to prevent.
fix_sketch: Replace the inline coercion with the same shape as safeBps: `feeBps === null || feeBps === undefined ? DEFAULT_FEE_BPS : (Number.isFinite(n) && n >= 0 && n <= 3000 ? Math.trunc(n) : DEFAULT_FEE_BPS)`. Better, import shared/pricing.js's earnerNetCents/coerceBps rather than keeping a fourth hand-written transcription of platform_fee_cents that no drift test covers (__tests__/pricing.test.js parses the migration against shared/pricing.js only).
verifier_note:
Severity low, not medium. Nothing is charged or paid wrongly — this is the assistant's advisory JSON only, and the error is in the conservative direction (the earner is told they earned $6.55/gig LESS than they were actually paid), so no user is induced to under-collect. It requires an operator to have launched a 0-bps campaign or enabled a 0-bps rung; none of the three seeded fee_tiers rungs is 0 and all three ship disabled. Real, worth fixing as a disclosure/drift defect — the same helper is a fourth hand-written transcription of platform_fee_cents that the drift test does not cover — but it is not in the same class as a mispriced charge.

One addition the finding misses: the same expression also fails to reject an out-of-range rate. safeBps rejects anything above 3000 bps; netOf accepts any positive number, so a corrupt or future out-of-range fee_bps_quoted would be reported as-is rather than falling back.

title: settle_booking_benefits has no promotion-kind filter: every poster-discount capture refunds the campaign's entire budget charge, so budget_cents stops bounding loss
summary: settle_booking_benefits (the FINAL and only definition, 20260806220000:155) loops over every promo_redemptions row for the booking with no `kind` discrimination and prices each one with promo_benefit_cents(), which is the FEE-OVERRIDE counterfactual (fee at the standing rate minus fee at r.fee_bps). For a poster_discount redemption, r.fee_bps is not a promo rate at all — consume_poster_discount stores the booking's own fee_bps_quoted there — so on the ordinary booking (no fee override in play) r.fee_bps == fee_bps_at(now()) and promo_benefit_cents returns 0. `actual` becomes 0, `delta` becomes -reserved_cents, and the UPDATE at :188-190 hands the campaign back the whole amount it was charged at booking. redemptions_used is NOT decremented, so the row still exists and looks settled, but promotions.spent_cents returns to ~0 after every capture. This is the same kind-confusion class that 20260806340000 fixed inside consume_poster_discount; the sibling settle function was never touched.
trigger: Enable the shipped `first_hire_discount` preset (kind='poster_discount', poster_discount_cents=1000, budget_cents=50000, max_redemptions=100, max_benefit_cents default 15000). A poster holding a grant books a $100 gig at the standing 1000 bps. consume_poster_discount: headroom = platform_fee_cents(10000,1000)=1000 minus floor 345 = 655; hit = least(1000, 655, 15000) = 655; promotions.spent_cents += 655; promo_redemptions row written with fee_bps = 1000 (20260806340000:124-126, the value the pin passed from new.fee_bps_quoted). The poster is charged 9345 and the platform keeps 345. At verify, stripe-capture-payment calls settle_booking_benefits(booking, 10000). r.fee_bps = 1000 = fee_bps_at(now()), so promo_benefit_cents(10000,1000) = 1000 - 1000 = 0; actual = least(15000, 0) = 0; delta = 0 - 655 = -655; spent_cents goes back to 0 and benefit_cents is recorded as 0. Repeat for every captured booking: spent_cents only ever reflects in-flight, uncaptured discounts.
money_impact: The platform. The documented loss bound for a campaign is 'budget_cents + max_redemptions' (20260806070000 header, 'Loss is bounded by construction'); after this, budget_cents binds only on concurrently-in-flight discounts and lifetime exposure becomes max_redemptions x per-use cap. On the shipped preset that is 100 x 655c = $655 against a $500 budget ($155 unbudgeted). An operator who sets a generous max_redemptions and relies on the dollar budget — which the console's own burn-down bar invites, admin/app/(console)/promotions/page.tsx:95 and :113 read spent_cents/budget_cents — overspends without limit up to the redemption count. Two corrections, both making the finding worse rather than better, plus one overstatement to trim.

EXPOSURE IS UNDERSTATED. The finding prices the leak at 100 x 655c = $655 against a $500 budget. 655c is only the headroom on a $100 gig. hit = least(poster_discount_cents, cap, max_benefit_cents), and for the shipped preset poster_discount_cents = 1000c. Headroom(a, 1000bps) = 0.10a - (ceil(0.029a) + 55), which reaches 1000c at roughly a = $149. Above that the full $10 is granted, so lifetime exposure on the first_hire_discount preset is 100 x 1000c = $1,000 against a $500 budget — 2x, not 1.31x.

THE PRESET IS OPERATOR-CREATED, NOT SEEDED. The finding says 'the shipped first_hire_discount preset'; it lives in admin/app/(console)/promotions/presets.ts:78-93 as a console form-filler, and createPromotion inserts it as status='draft'. So the trigger requires an admin to create AND activate it. That is the intended supported workflow (it is the only poster-side preset offered), so it does not refute — but the finding reads as though a live campaign already exists, and none is seeded by any migration.

THE MECHANISM CLAIM ABOUT r.fee_bps IS RIGHT BUT SLIGHTLY NARROW. r.fee_bps == fee_bps_at(now()) holds only while the standing rate is unchanged between booking and capture. If platform_rates gains a higher future-dated row that takes effect in between, promo_benefit_cents returns a positive number that is the RATE-CHANGE delta, not the discount — still unrelated to the discount actually delivered, so the accounting is wrong in that case too, just not always a clean zero.

Secondary effects both check out as stated: the console burn-down bar (promotions/page.tsx:95 computes pct from spent_cents/budget_cents, :113 renders it) permanently reads ~$0.00, and the 'budget can't go below what's already committed' refusal (promotions/actions.ts:160-168) reads the same reset spent_cents, so it is toothless — I confirmed cur.spent_cents is the only value it compares against.

title: An earner's vested referral fee credit is consumed in full but delivered only in part (or not at all), and is never restored after a partial capture, a refund, or a chargeback
summary: consume_fee_credit flips bonus_ledger rows to state='applied' at booking INSERT. The only code path in the repo that ever flips them back is release_booking_benefits, which runs solely from the declined/cancelled status trigger and early-returns whenever any payment on the booking is captured. So three ordinary outcomes destroy earned credit: a partial capture delivers only pct of it while burning 100%; a full refund or chargeback delivers none of it while burning 100%; and a booking left 'pending' forever holds it hostage with no release path at all. No control covers any of the three.
trigger: (a) PARTIAL CAPTURE. Earner holds a vested $6.55 credit. $100 gig, 1000 bps: F=1000, floor=345, headroom=655, so the whole 655c row is flipped to 'applied' and fee_credit_cents=655. Poster reports a problem and captures at pct=0.5. stripe-capture-payment:150 computes fullFeeCalc = platform_fee_after_credit(10000, 1000, 655) = 345; :179 feeCents = round(345 * 0.5) = 173. Without the credit the fee would have been round(1000*0.5) = 500. Value delivered to the earner = 327c; value consumed = 655c. 328c evaporates into the platform's fee. (b) REFUND/CHARGEBACK. Same booking captured in full: the credit is delivered (fee 1000 -> 345). An admin then refunds in full, or the poster charges back. record_refund reverses the earner's net and Stripe's refund_application_fee returns the platform's fee. Net money movement is zero on all three sides — but the bonus_ledger row stays state='applied' with applied_booking_id pointing at a 'verified' booking, so the credit is gone. (c) GHOSTED APPLICATION. Earner applies to a gig, the credit is consumed at INSERT, the poster never answers. The booking sits 'pending' indefinitely (ctl_stranded_pending_booking documents that nothing expires one) and release_booking_benefits never fires because it is wired only to declined/cancelled.
money_impact: The earner loses up to the full face value of a bonus they earned by referring a real person who completed real work (promotions.bonus_cents, admin-set). The platform keeps the difference, so it is a transfer from worker to platform. The user-facing receipt actively misstates it: src/screens/PaymentsScreen.js:417 renders 'Fee credit applied + $6.55' from payments.fee_credit_cents — the amount CONSUMED — on a booking where only $3.27 of benefit reached them. Detection gap: ctl_credit_stranded_on_dead_booking (20260806260000) requires bk.status in ('declined','cancelled') AND no captured payment, so it matches none of (a), (b) or (c). vest_bonuses proves the refund linkage was modelled in the other direction only — it voids state='pending' bonuses whose source booking was refunded, but nothing claws back or restores an 'applied' one.
fix_sketch: Two changes. (1) On a partial capture, restore the undelivered portion: settle the credit alongside the promo in the same settle_booking_benefits call — split the bonus_ledger row and return round(credit * (1-pct)) to state='payable'. (2) Extend release to reversal: when record_refund brings refunded_cents up to the captured total, restore the credit pro rata, and broaden ctl_credit_stranded_on_dead_booking to also match bookings whose payment is fully refunded and bookings still 'pending' past the stranded-application window.
verifier_note: Two corrections and a downgrade to medium. (1) Sub-claim (c) — the 'ghosted pending booking holds the credit hostage with no release path' — is REFUTED. There is a self-service path: JobsContext.cancelBooking (src/context/JobsContext.js:753) lets either party cancel from 'pending', which sets status='cancelled', fires trg_zz_release_benefits, and (with no captured payment) restores the credit to 'payable'. The earner can withdraw the application and get the credit back; this is a discoverability problem, not a permanent loss. (2) The mechanism of the (a) loss is stated slightly wrong. 'The platform keeps the difference' is not accurate for the booking in question — the platform DID give up 327c of fee on it (173c collected instead of 500c). What is actually destroyed is the RESIDUAL: ~328c of vested credit that can never be applied to any future booking, because the row is fully burned and never split back. Note also that the honest ceiling on a 50% capture is lower than the finding implies — applying the credit to the partial basis directly would give platform_fee_after_credit(5000,1000,655) = 200c (floor-bound), i.e. at most ~300c deliverable — so the earner actually received slightly MORE benefit on this booking than the credit could strictly deliver, and the loss is purely the unreturned remainder. Severity medium rather than high: the per-event loss is capped at the credit's face value, it requires a dispute-path partial capture or a reversal, and the most common outcome (full capture) delivers the credit in full.
